CVE-2026-97033.description: Building a malicious package that uses cgo could cause arbitrary code execution at build time through several compiler and linker flags permitted in "#cgo" directives. Specifically, "--sysroot" in GCC and Clang relocates compiler subprograms, spec files, and CRT startup objects to an attacker-controlled directory; "-target" in Clang falls back to executing target helper tools from the current working directory when not found in PATH; "-isysroot" and "-Wl,-syslibroot" can pass a regular file on disk to GNU ld.bfd, which interprets it as a positional linker script; and "-x" permitted specifying arbitrary compiler input languages beyond those supported by cgo. "--sysroot" and "-target" are now disallowed in "#cgo" flags, "-isysroot" and "-Wl,-syslibroot" are verified not to point to regular files, and "-x" is restricted to the C, C++, Objective-C, and assembler languages supported by cgo.

🐧 SIGINT // Ubuntu Watch — 2026-11-12

Primary source from Canonical on a Linux kernel CVE. Fixes sit in the proposed pocket, so they are not in stable updates yet. Homelabbers can test them on a non-critical box, or wait for the stable release, and plan a reboot. Don't rely on upstream fix status alone.

🔗 https://ubuntu.com/blog/fixes-available-in-proposed-pocket-for-cve-2026-98432

#Ubuntu #Linux #infosec

CVE-2026-98432.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period

tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the
child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it.

Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same
request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req().
tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt
under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and
ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice.

Note that the SYNACK timer itself is not an issue: it holds a
reference on its request socket, and inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop()
calls timer_delete_sync() before the child can be freed.

Since commit 079096f103fa ("tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests
into ehash table"), request sockets are processed without holding
the listener lock, so nothing prevents the child socket from being
freed while the SYNACK is still being built. TCP child sockets do
not have SOCK_RCU_FREE, and inet_sock_destruct() frees inet_opt
with a plain kfree(), leading to a use-after-free in
ip_options_build().

A similar issue exists with request socket migration
(net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE
program). reqsk_timer_handler() clones the request socket with
inet_reqsk_clone(), so that the old request socket and its clone
share the same ireq_opt, then reqsk_migrate_reset() clears the
pointer in the old one. Another cpu holding a reference on the old
request socket can still be using these options (sending a SYNACK,
or creating a child in tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock()) when the clone is
freed, and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() also uses a plain kfree().

Readers already use RCU, and other paths replacing inet_opt
(do_ip_setsockopt(), cipso_v4_sock_setattr()...) already use
kfree_rcu(). Use kfree_rcu() in inet_sock_destruct() and
tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() as well.

IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock()
duplicates the options. tcp_v6_reqsk_destructor() has the same
migration issue with ipv6_opt, which is only set by CALIPSO. This
will be addressed in a separate patch.

In version 1.7.3, ApprovalResourceService.sendWebHook reads WebHookConfig.webHookUrl from stored approval-node configuration and passes it through ApprovalFlowService.updateApprovalPostField to HttpClientUtils without the SSRF validation used by the optional testConnect path. A user with PROCESS_SETTING_ADD can configure an internal URL through POST /approval-flow/add and cause the server to request it when POST /approval-action/approve executes the approval action, enabling cloud metadata access, internal network reconnaissance, and interaction with reachable internal services. This issue is fixed in version 1.7.4.

posts.content:
The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2

In this article
  1. When one RCE stops being just one RCE
  2. Observed attack chains
  3. How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket
  4. How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address
  5. Mitigation and protection guidance
  6. References
  7. Learn More

Microsoft observed multiple incidents in which threat actors deployed GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers. Threat actors used Gsocket to maintain access even after the vulnerabilities used for initial compromise were remediated. This turned a single web application compromise into persistent access that outlasted the remediation of the original vulnerabilities. Defenders investigating affected hosts should look for evidence of GSocket deployment, persistence, privilege escalation, and outbound connections, rather than treating application patching alone as complete remediation.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows this activity growing over recent months and concentrated on web applications and hosting environments. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block.

When one RCE stops being just one RCE

Exploiting a web application vulnerability gives a threat actor command execution in the context of the web server process. That access lasts only while the vulnerability remains unpatched and the service keeps running. Patching the application or restarting the service can remove it.

To keep access, threat actors typically add a persistence mechanism, and each common option has drawbacks. SSH keys added to authorized_keys are easy for administrators to find during an audit. Reverse shells depend on threat actor-controlled servers that defenders can block or sinkhole. Custom implants require ongoing development and maintenance. The same trade-offs apply when initial access comes through remote access services or cloud shell sessions.

GSocket addresses these drawbacks, which helps explain why multiple unrelated threat actors have adopted it.

  • Shared relay infrastructure. Traffic passes through the Global Socket Relay Network, a public relay service. The threat actor does not register or host any infrastructure, so there is no threat actor-owned IP address or domain to block. Organizations can still restrict access to the relay itself.
  • Outbound-only connections. The compromised host and the operator both connect outbound to the relay, which bridges the two sessions. The host needs no inbound listener or public IP address, and network address translation does not prevent the connection. Inbound firewall rules do not see this traffic, although egress filtering and outbound monitoring can.
  • Built-in evasion and persistence. The deployment script can rename the process, stage files in memory-backed directories, and install persistence that survives a reboot, without additional development by the threat actor.

The same relay model that supports legitimate remote administration also gives threat actors a way to maintain access without operating dedicated C2 infrastructure. Once GSocket runs on a compromised server, the server and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an end-to-end encrypted channel.

Figure 1: After code execution on an internet-facing application, GSocket is deployed and both ends connect outward to the relay.

Because GSocket runs independently of the exploited application, patching the vulnerability does not remove the relay client or its persistence.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint telemetry shows that this activity is not limited to a single compromise. From March through August 2026, devices with GSocket-related detections increased 356.2%, although the increase was not consistent month to month.

Figure 2: Growth in GSocket-related detections from March to August, measured against the March baseline.

Web applications and hosting accounted for 87.1% of attributable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint incidents in the analysed telemetry. Within that group, PHP web applications and cPanel hosting represented 63.9% of incidents and Apache represented 24.3% (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Distribution of GSocket-related incidents by application category. PHP web applications and Apache account for most incidents within the web applications and hosting group.

Education and research accounted for the largest share of affected organizations (30.7%), followed by technology and telecommunications (22.9%).

Figure 4: Distribution of affected organizations by sector.

These figures reflect the share of affected organizations and do not indicate that threat actors selected these sectors deliberately. Exposure is the more likely factor: academic institutions often run large, decentralized web estates maintained outside central IT, which are harder to inventory and patch.

Observed attack chains

The RCE-based intrusions in this analysis followed a similar sequence after initial access. Threat actors compromised an internet-facing application, profiled the host, transferred and concealed the relay tooling, and used the resulting channel for command and control. Some intrusions also included persistence and privilege escalation. Figure 5 combines these behaviours into a generalized attack chain. Not every stage occurred in every intrusion.

Figure 5: Generalized GSocket attack chain observed across RCE-based intrusions, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. How threat actors deploy and operate GSocket

Initial access and deployment: Threat actors exploited internet-facing web applications and used curl to download and execute a remote script. The script profiled the host, selected a GSocket client matching the system architecture, staged it in writable or memory-backed paths such as /dev/shm, and established encrypted outbound command and control through the Global Socket Relay Network.

Figure 6: Encoded RCE command executed through a vulnerable PHP application.

Defense evasion and persistence: Threat actors disguised GSocket with kernel-thread-like process names, persisted through cron, systemd, shell profiles, watchdogs, and redundant copies, then removed staging files and other deployment indicators.

Figure 7: Kernel thread names used to disguise the GSocket process. Figure 8: Persistence entries created during GSocket deployment.

Privilege escalation: After gaining execution as the web-service account, in few observed incidents, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284, one of the recent Linux kernel vulnerabilities also known as Dirty Frag, to elevate privileges to root.

How GSocket reconnects without a fixed C2 address

GSocket identifies endpoints by a shared secret instead of an IP address or hostname. During installation, the deployment script typically generates a random secret and writes it to standard output. The threat actor can choose to read the secret from the console, redirect it to a temporary file and retrieve the file before is deleted, or have it delivered through a supported notification channel, such as Telegram (configured with GS_TG_TOKEN and GS_TG_CHATID), Discord, or a webhook. With this secret, the operator can reconnect later from any compatible GSocket client, without knowing the victim’s IP address, hostname, or network location.

A traditional reverse shell connects to a threat actor-controlled IP address written into the payload. GSocket instead derives its connection identifier and authentication material from the shared secret. The compromised host and the operator each connect outbound to the Global Socket Relay Network (GSRN), which matches them and brokers an end-to-end encrypted session. Neither endpoint needs a public IP address, an inbound listener, or a permissive inbound firewall rule.

As a result, blocking an IP address or domain is unlikely to cut off access. The connection relies on a shared relay service, outbound traffic that is commonly permitted, and a secret that does not need to be hardcoded in the payload. Anyone with the shared secret can reconnect through the relay without knowing the compromised host’s IP address or hostname.

Mitigation and protection guidance

For an affected Linux server, remediation should address both the initial compromise and the GSocket deployment.

  1. Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.
    • Remediate the host as well as the vulnerability. Do not treat application patching as complete remediation. Investigate and remove the GSocket client, associated persistence, and staged files, then verify that outbound connections to the relay infrastructure have stopped
  2. Patch and harden internet-facing applications. Keep web applications, CMS platforms, plugins, and application servers current. Remove unused components and restrict file-upload and administrative paths.
  3. Constrain outbound traffic. Apply deny-by-default egress rules, allow only required destinations, and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.
  4. Harden the host runtime. Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable where feasible, and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.
  5. Audit persistence surfaces. Review cron entries, systemd units with plausible service names, and shell startup files. Persistence is often layered across several mechanisms, so stopping the running process alone does not remove access.
  6. Prioritize local privilege-escalation patching on internet-facing servers. In the analyzed activity, threat actors attempted to exploit CVE-2026-43284 to escalate from the web-service account to root. Separately, Microsoft FORGE Lab recently documented 59 Linux kernel bug reports, including eight vulnerabilities for which researchers demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled environments.
  7. Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux. Keep real-time and cloud-delivered protection enabled, with behavior monitoring for anomalous child processes of web services and masqueraded process identities.
Microsoft Defender detections

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint provides visibility into activity associated with GSocket-related Linux intrusions, including suspicious shell execution, payload delivery, persistence, defense evasion, and remote communication. The alerts below were observed in the analyzed telemetry. An individual alert does not establish the initial access method or confirm that every stage of an intrusion succeeded.

TacticObserved activityExample alerts observed in analyzed telemetryInitial access, ExecutionShells and commands launched from web servers and application runtimes– Possible Web Server compromise activity

– Suspicious shell execution from web server application

– Suspicious remote command execution via Java Web application

Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

  • Incident investigation: correlate web-service process ancestry, relay client deployment, persistence changes, and outbound activity into a single timeline for the affected host.
  • Threat actor profile: summarize observed GSocket tradecraft and related tooling seen in the environment.
  • Device summary: assess the affected Linux host, its exposed application, and follow-on activity after initial execution.
Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following queries to surface GSocket-related activity. The queries use public Advanced Hunting tables populated by Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and cover deployment patterns observed in the analyzed intrusions.

Matches should be investigated in context with process ancestry, execution context, persistence changes, and related network activity.

GSocket process activity

Looks for GSocket tooling by name or command line.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has_any ("gs-netcat", "gsocket")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gsocket.io", "gs-netcat", "gsnetcat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
    ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

Installer download activity

Looks for the download-and-execute pattern used to fetch GSocket.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gsocket.io"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "gsgg.b-cdn.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
    ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

Connections to observed distribution hosts

These are tool distribution endpoints, not threat actor-owned command and control.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("gsocket.io", "gsgg.b-cdn.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

Known file hashes

Matches the SHA-256 hashes published in the indicators of compromise section.

let badSHA256 = dynamic([
    "d94f75a70b5cabaf786ac57177ed841732e62bdcc9a29e06e5b41d9be567bcfa",
    "f95c4d029e6784e3849b4d1e2e2ae1a661187236ef7c5d487c71158a290a03b5",
    "55d141bb2f62c527c3fea3413b8429fed7d52633d0b123b5e611bfa42165229f",
    "12450bafc7a4398040e1ad3a16dbf4dbc79b6a8f83ef306c4f0f73f59886f06c"
]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where SHA256 in~ (badSHA256)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Staging and persistence artifacts

Useful when hashes are missing or a different build is used.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/.gs-"
    or FileName in~ ("systemd-remount-d", ".gsn_ora", "defunct", "defunct.service")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
    InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed

The following techniques were observed across the analyzed intrusions. Not every technique occurred in every intrusion, and some outcomes, such as persistence across reboot and successful relay session establishment, were not confirmed in every case.

Initial access

  • T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application | Internet-facing web applications were exploited to gain command execution in the web service context. Follow-on commands were launched as children of web server and application runtime processes, consistent with exploitation of an exposed application.

Execution

  • T1059.004 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell | Commands used curl to retrieve the GSocket installation script and executed it with bash.
    Additional bash invocations launched the renamed payload.

Execution, Persistence

  • T1053.003 Scheduled Task/Job: Cron | Cron entries were created in the same detection window as GSocket deployment script activity, consistent with persistence.

Persistence

  • T1543.002 Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service | Activity launched a bash command invoking the renamed /usr/bin/defunct payload and referenced defunct.service and a multi-user.target.wants link.

Defense evasion

  • T1036 Masquerading | A GsNetcat binary executed as systemd-remount-d, a system service-like filename. In a separate execution context, bash used exec -a to present /usr/bin/defunct with the argument-zero name [kaluad].
  • T1564.001 Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories | gs-netcat payloads were staged under the dot-prefixed /dev/shm/.gs-0 directory. A GsNetcat-detected file was also observed at /tmp/.gsn_ora.
  • T1222.002 File and Directory Permissions Modification: Linux and Mac File and Directory Permissions Modification | chmod changed permissions on the renamed payload, including chmod 700 /usr/bin/defunct.
  • T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp | touch commands applied older timestamps to /usr/bin/defunct and defunct.service. Timestamp copy operations targeted the system service-like payload name.
  • T1070.004 Indicator Removal: File Deletion | rm removed the staged /dev/shm/.gs-0/gs-netcat file, and a separate rmdir command removed the staging directory.

Command and control

  • T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer | curl downloaded gs-netcat payloads from GSocket distribution endpoints into /dev/shm/.gs-0.
  • T1090.002 Proxy: External Proxy | GSocket clients were launched with options that establish outbound sessions to the Global Socket Relay Network, a shared public relay that brokers the connection between the compromised host and the operator. The relay is third-party infrastructure and is not owned by the threat actor.

CVE-2026-43284.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm: esp: avoid in-place decrypt on shared skb frags

MSG_SPLICE_PAGES can attach pages from a pipe directly to an skb. TCP
marks such skbs with SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG after skb_splice_from_iter(),
so later paths that may modify packet data can first make a private
copy. The IPv4/IPv6 datagram append paths did not set this flag when
splicing pages into UDP skbs.

That leaves an ESP-in-UDP packet made from shared pipe pages looking
like an ordinary uncloned nonlinear skb. ESP input then takes the no-COW
fast path for uncloned skbs without a frag_list and decrypts in place
over data that is not owned privately by the skb.

Mark IPv4/IPv6 datagram splice frags with SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG, matching
TCP. Also make ESP input fall back to skb_cow_data() when the flag is
present, so ESP does not decrypt externally backed frags in place.
Private nonlinear skb frags still use the existing fast path.

This intentionally does not change ESP output. In esp_output_head(),
the path that appends the ESP trailer to existing skb tailroom without
calling skb_cow_data() is not reachable for nonlinear skbs:
skb_tailroom() returns zero when skb->data_len is nonzero, while ESP
tailen is positive. Thus ESP output will either use the separate
destination-frag path or fall back to skb_cow_data().

CVE-2026-123864.description: A re-entrancy flaw in Node.js HTTPS lets an unauthenticated client read memory belonging to other connections, including TLS private keys and other users' requests. TLSWrap::DoWrite() calls ClearOut() directly when asked to write zero bytes; if that write is issued from JavaScript running inside the HTTP parser's on_body callback, ClearOut() decrypts the next TLS record while the parser is still mid-body, re-entering llhttp_execute() and causing a use-after-free and an out-of-bounds heap read. The server then copies that freed or unrelated heap memory into the response for the request body. Triggering it requires a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body ends and later calls res.end() with a non-empty chunk, and reading the leaked memory requires any ordinary route that echoes or stores a request body. Cleartext node:http is not affected. This vulnerability affects Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

posts.content:
I found an API key leak in MLflow, and why your AI agent may have one too

MLflow에서 CrewAI 자동 로깅(mlflow.crewai.autolog())을 켜면 에이전트가 LLM 제공자(OpenAI, Anthropic 등)를 호출할 때 쓰는 API 키가 trace에 함께 기록되는 문제가 발견되어 CVE-2026-116691로 등록됐다. 앱이 키를 로깅한 것이 아니라 계측 코드가 기록했고, 키는 MLflow 추적 백엔드와 trace를 내보낸 다른 시스템에 남는다. 영향 범위는 MLflow 2.19.0부터 3.16.x까지이며 3.17.0(PR #25845)에서 수정됐다. 업그레이드해도 이미 기록된 키는...

https://github.com/ralis-ai/weir/blob/main/docs/cve-2026-116691.md

CVE-2026-116691.description: MLflow is an open source AI engineering platform for agents, large language models, and machine learning models. From 2.19.0 until 3.17.0, mlflow.crewai.autolog() records CrewAI Agent objects without consistently sanitizing nested credential-bearing values. mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_get_agent_attributes() converts the Agent llm field to a string that includes the provider API key, while mlflow/crewai/autolog.py::_construct_full_inputs() expands the Agent object into mlflow.spanInputs. Applications can therefore send plaintext provider credentials to the MLflow trace backend or a configured OTLP destination, where trace readers can obtain them. This issue is fixed in version 3.17.0.

posts.content:
🚨 Public exploit code is out for CVE-2026-126187, a critical unauthenticated Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting React Server Components and certain Next.js applications.

Scored CVSS 9.5, the flaw could allow remote attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers without authentication.

The catch? Not every React or Next.js application is vulnerable. Exploitation requires a specific configuration involving Next.js Cache Components ("use cache"), multiple typed arrays sharing an underlying buffer, and an attacker-controlled value.

The vulnerability exploits a React Flight deserialization flaw that can be turned into Server Action execution through a crafted HTTP GET request.

⚠️ Patches have been available since October 14, 2026. Yet npm data showed 73% of recent "react-server-dom-webpack" downloads were still using affected versions as of November 11.

Technical breakdown, exploit mechanics, affected versions and detection:
https://thecybersecguru.com/exploits/cve-2026-126187-react-flight-rce/

#CyberSecurity #InfoSec #ReactJS #NextJS #RCE #CVE2026126187 #AppSec

CVE-2026-126187.description:
### Impact

Crafted payloads targeting frameworks supporting React Server Components can lead to remote code execution. This only affects extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value.

Updating immediately is recommended.

The vulnerability exists in versions 19.0.0 through 19.0.8, 19.1.0 through 19.1.9, 19.2.0 through 19.2.8 and 19.3.0 of:

- react-server-dom-webpack
- react-server-dom-parcel
- react-server-dom-turbopack

### Patches

Fixes were back ported to versions 19.0.09, 19.1.10, 19.2.9, and 19.3.1.

If applications are using any of the above packages please upgrade to any of the fixed versions immediately.

If an app’s React code does not use a server, the app is not affected by this vulnerability. If an app does not use a framework, bundler, or bundler plugin that supports React Server Components, the app is not affected by this vulnerability.

posts.content: CVE-2026-63349 AnyIO 4.14.0 forwards the wrong argument, so extra_groups=[] fails to drop inherited supplementary groups, undermining privilege dropping. CVSS 3.6. Patch under review, so track it and update as soon as it lands. https://www.valtersit.com/cve/CVE-2026-63349/

CVE-2026-63349.description: AnyIO 4.14.0 accepts the POSIX extra_groups argument on anyio.run_process() and anyio.open_process(), but open_process() forwards the wrong variable to the backend: when extra_groups is not None, it assigns kwargs["extra_groups"] = group instead of extra_groups. As a result, callers cannot reliably clear or set supplementary groups for child processes. In a disposable Linux container, Python's subprocess.run(..., extra_groups=[]) clears a synthetic parent supplementary group list, while anyio.run_process(..., extra_groups=[]) preserves the parent groups. If group is also supplied, AnyIO passes an integer as extra_groups and the call fails with TypeError. This is a POSIX privilege-dropping correctness issue for applications that rely on AnyIO subprocess helpers to launch less-privileged child processes.
